props.title: Stonewall

sections.content: The 1995 film Stonewall tackles the pivotal 1969 Stonewall riots but stumbles in its execution. While groundbreaking for its time as one of the first mainstream films to address this watershed moment in LGBTQ+ history, it falls into the trap of centering a fictional white protagonist rather than the actual trans women of color like Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera who were key figures in the uprising. This approach mirrors similar issues seen in Milk (2008) and Philadelphia (1993) - early gay rights films that, while important, played it relatively safe for mainstream audiences.

sections.content: The 1990s saw a surge of New Queer Cinema that offered more authentic representations than Stonewall. Paris Is Burning (1990) masterfully documented NYC's ballroom culture. The Living End (1992) and Swoon (1992) brought unapologetic queer narratives to indie audiences. These films rejected sanitized mainstream portrayals in favor of raw authenticity.

More recent films have better honored Stonewall's legacy. Pride (2014) brilliantly depicts the alliance between Welsh miners and LGBTQ+ activists. BPM (Beats Per Minute) (2017) powerfully captures the urgency of ACT UP's AIDS activism. Happy Birthday, Marsha! (2018) finally gives Marsha P. Johnson's story the respect it deserves. movies.slug: Experimental short imagining Marsha P. Johnson the night before Stonewall

sections.content: While Stonewall largely erased trans voices, films like Disclosure (2020) have thoroughly examined Hollywood's problematic history with trans representation. Paris Is Burning (1990) and The Queen (1968) provided early authentic glimpses into trans life, though through a documentary lens. Narrative breakthroughs finally came with Boys Don't Cry (1999), A Fantastic Woman (2017), and Tangerine (2015) centering trans protagonists played by trans actors.
